title: Slate a take: hold a clapperboard square to the phone camera and clap its stick shut once, sharply
instruction: Slate the take: hold the clapperboard facing the phone camera, fully in its frame, and clap its stick shut once, sharply.
context: Slating a take is the clapperboard moment everyone knows from film sets and behind-the-scenes clips, now common in phone filming too: the frame where the sticks meet is lined up with the clap's sound. A slating guide: "Proper slating technique dictates holding the slate with one hand and closing the clapper with the other"; "THE SLATE MUST NOT MOVE WHILE THE CLAPPER IS IN MOTION"; motion blur makes it "very hard to figure out when the clapper stops moving". Here the 5 mm acrylic slate cannot stand by itself (it leans on a case, 28 deg off the camera's axis, and falls back when let go), so one hand must hold it upright, square to the lens and still, while the other opens the stick and drives it shut fast: the hinge's tension screw holds the stick where it is left, so letting go does not clap it. One arm alone cannot both hold the board and work the stick.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Acrylic film clapperboard (like the Neewer 30 x 25 cm acrylic clapboard), loose: black writing board 30.0 x 20.0 cm, 5 mm thick, printed with white lines; a fixed lower clapstick 30.0 x 2.5 cm, 8 mm thick, along its top edge; the upper clapstick (same size, white with black stripes) on a hinge pin 1 cm in from the board's left end (robot's view), free end on the robot's right; 30 x 25 cm overall, 0.52 kg (upper stick 0.07 kg). The hinge's tension screw holds the stick open at any angle (0.12 N m of friction); the stick opens up to 45 deg. Stick shut, the slate stands on its bottom edge, the middle of that edge at x 27, y 2, its face toward +x (the phone), leaning back 28 deg with its back on the case's far top edge (its top edge at x 15.5, 22 cm up). (2) Hard plastic equipment case, loose, 2.0 kg: 20 (x) x 16 (y) x 15 cm tall, x -1 to 19, y -6 to 10. (3) Phone on a tabletop tripod, fixed: landscape, its lens at x 70, y 2, 13 cm up, looking straight back along -x; 16:9 video, 69 x 43 deg field of view (26 mm-equivalent main camera), 240 captured frames per second. (4) A strip of tape on the table along the camera's axis, x 38 to 58, y 2. Both arms start at the ready pose, grippers open. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Read every physics step (240 Hz): the stick's angle and the slate's pose. A clap: the stick shuts (within 1 deg of closed) after being open 20 deg or more; any later shut after it was opened 10 deg or more is another clap. The first clap is the take's sync mark and is judged. 0: no clap in the run; or at the first clap the slate's face is more than 20 deg off the camera's axis (slate middle to lens) or a corner of the slate is outside the camera's 69 x 43 deg view. 0.5: the first clap faces the camera and is in frame, but it was slow (more than 50 ms from 10 deg open to shut), or the slate's middle moved 1 cm or more over the 0.25 s before and after it, or there was more than one clap in the run. 1.0 (success, held 1 s): one clap only, facing and in frame, from 10 deg to shut within 50 ms, the slate still within 1 cm. Why 50 ms: a 24 fps film frame lasts 41.7 ms; a stick that crosses its last 10 deg within about one frame gives a clean sync frame. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: use the phone's original 240 fps capture frames. Let i be the last frame at least 10 deg open before the first clap (about a 5.0 cm tip gap), and j the first later frame within 1 deg of shut (about a 5 mm tip gap). Time is (j - i) / 240 seconds, so 12 frame intervals pass. Use capture fps for slow-motion exports. Read slate movement against the printed lines and tape. Check that the whole slate is in the phone frame and count the claps on video. Read facing from the overhead video against the tape.
reset_notes: Shut the stick, lean the slate on the case as in the screenshot (bottom edge 27 cm in front of the arm bases, centred 2 cm left, leaning back 28 deg), check the case is in place and the phone is capturing 240 fps and the overhead camera is recording, arms at the ready pose. Simulation: each trial starts the simulator afresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 20 Hz control, scored at 240 Hz. Board 5 mm and sticks 8 mm, as boxes; the hinge is a joint with 0.12 N m Coulomb friction (estimate of a tightened tension screw) and its shut stop is the joint's limit (the sticks, one articulation, do not collide with each other), so there is no bounce. No sound: the clap is read from the hinge's angle. The phone's view is a pinhole check of the slate's corners, not a render. The case is a plain box.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both grippers went to the slate and took hold of its two ends, tipping it back flat onto the case; the stick was never opened and there was no clap); demo: 1.0
